text: Cent #189.
Cards, sneakers, watches and coins
are graded and traded like securities,
and a grade rewards an object
for how little has happened to it.
The collectors of CENTS value
what happened to each coin.
In a conversation in her 2022
book Proof of Work, Rhea Myers quotes
Barbara Kruger: "Money is an information-destroying medium."
A circulated copper cent is the exception.
Its wear and patina record where it has been.
In the image of Cent #189,
that record is red, a trait called Full Red.
In the Traits Atlas, red patina is "a red
to reddish-brown surface film resulting
from oxidative conversion of copper,"
and Full Red means red is the dominant
surface condition,
generally over about seventy percent of the coin.
Seventy-one Cents are Full Red.
Cent #189 is the only one
dated 1960.
Pale, sandy films of Notable Desert
lie on Lincoln's hair, cheek and coat:
clearly visible, but local,
up to about a fifth of the surface.
Compare Cent #189 with Cent #9794,
also a 1960 with a D mark, and close to mint state.
As money, any cent was as good as any other.
As a Cent, none is.
A Cent's worth is set by the people who keep,
exchange, catalog and compare
it, and set again each time.
Cent #189, a great Cent.
